item.title: SonicWall Warns Gen 6 Firewalls Won't Get Security Patches, Even for Critical Flaws (2026)
item.description:
SonicWall has urged all customers still running Generation 6 firewalls to retire and replace them immediately and stop exposing the devices on the internet edge, citing security risks fueled by AI-assisted attacks.

"Attackers now use automation and AI to find and exploit unsupported edge devices faster than ever," SonicWall said. "We expect internet-facing Gen 6 firewalls to be actively targeted. Treat any Gen 6 firewall still in service as a high-risk exposure, and migrate to a supported Gen 8 firewall running SonicOS 8."

The affected products running SonicOS 6.x include -

  • TZ350, TZ350W, TZ500, TZ500W, SOHO 250, SOHO 250W 
  • NSA 4600, NSA 5600, NSA 6600 
  • NSa 4650, NSa 5650, NSa 6650 
  • TZ400, TZ400W, TZ600, TZ600P, NSA 3600 
  • NSa 3650 
  • NSa 2650 
  • SOHO, SOHO W, TZ300P, NSa 9250, NSa 9450, NSa 9650 
  • NSv 10 to NSv 1600 (Gen 6 virtual) 
  • SuperMassive 9200, 9400, 9600, 9800 
  • NSsp 12800, NSsp 12400 
  • TZ300, TZ300W 
  • NSA 2600

In recent years, threat actors have increasingly targeted edge devices as a launch point to obtain initial access, even as the window between disclosure and confirmed exploitation has collapsed significantly, in part driven by threat actors' use of automation and AI to scan the internet for unsupported devices, analyze patches and vulnerability disclosure announcements, and build working exploits faster.

According to Google Mandiant's M-Trends report published in March 2026, the mean time to exploit vulnerabilities has turned negative,reaching an estimated -7 days – meaning exploitation, on average, begins before a patch is available – compared with 63 days in 2018 and -1 day in 2024.

"This trend is compounded by threat actors' evolving interest in security appliances and networking infrastructure," Google said. "Because these assets provide critical inspection of data ingress and egress points, they grant significant visibility and permissions to those who gain access to them."

Cisco Talos' 2025 Year in Review report has also found that 23% of CVEs discovered in the year directly impact network devices like VPN appliances, next-generation firewalls (NGFWs), load balancers, routers, and others.

"Since these systems sit at the perimeter of enterprise environments, compromise may lead to direct access to the critical networks," Talos said. "This aligns with real-world trends from CISA's Known Exploitation Vulnerability (KEV) catalog, where exploitation consistently favors edge devices because they are internetfacing, often lag in patching, and provide direct operational leverage once compromised."

With Gen 6 no longer being actively supported and receiving patches, even for critical flaws, users are recommended to follow the steps below without any delay -

  • Inventory every Gen 6 firewall in the production environment and retire them.
  • Prioritize units that are exposed to the internet or provide remote access.
  • Replace them with a Gen 8 firewall running SonicOS 8
  • Contact an authorized SonicWall partner to plan the migration

Until the firewall is replaced, it's advised to take the below actions to minimize exposure -

  • Disable WAN management (HTTPS, SSH, and SNMP on WAN interfaces).
  • Disable SSL VPN, or restrict it to known source addresses. 
  • Enforce multi-factor authentication on every remaining remote-access and admin account, and reset local passwords. 
  • Disable services and interfaces not in use.
  • Monitor logs closely for unusual logins, configuration changes and traffic.

"The risk to an unsupported firewall grows every day it stays online," SonicWall said. "One breach reaches everything. A compromised perimeter firewall gives attackers a foothold for credential theft, lateral movement and ransomware deployment."

item.title: The Path to AI Autonomy in the SOC (2026)
item.description:
Security leaders are about to hand AI agents a lot more authority. In a recent a16z survey of CISOs at organizations with more than 1,000 employees, 36% said they are comfortable today letting AI agents act autonomously on low-risk security actions. In 12 months from now, 60% expect to be comfortable at that level. Overall, AI SOC was the highest ranking initiative for 2027.

The pressure behind the shift is easy to see. In the same survey, the most common worry was AI-accelerated attacks outpacing the team's ability to respond, selected by 55% of respondents. Analyst time is the scarcest resource in the SOC, and every alert still means pulling evidence from several systems, reconstructing what happened and deciding whether it matters.

The same respondents are cautious at the top end. Only 1% are comfortable with agents acting autonomously on most actions today, and only 7% expect to be a year from now. Most teams want more autonomy, just not all of it.

Discussions today frame autonomy as a single slider that runs from "AI suggests" to "AI acts," and that exact framing is why so many programs stall. Autonomy is a set of decisions made per stage of the workflow and per action, and the teams that get it right treat it as something an agent earns with evidence.

Autonomy is not “all or nothing”, but rather a spectrum

The question "how much do we trust the AI" is too broad to answer. Researchers worked this out decades ago, in a framework later applied widely in aviation and air traffic control, long before anyone was building SOC agents.

In a widely cited 2000 paper, Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens proposed that automation applies to four broad functions. Those are information acquisition, information analysis, decision and action selection, and action implementation. Each function can sit at a different level of automation, from fully manual to fully automatic, within the same system.

Mapped onto security operations, the four stages look like this.

  1. Evidence collection. Querying the SIEM and EDR, pulling process trees, enriching indicators, gathering identity and cloud context.
  2. Analysis and verdict. Correlating what was collected, reconstructing what happened and deciding whether the alert is a real threat.
  3. Response recommendation. Proposing what should happen next, such as containing a host, resetting credentials or closing the case.
  4. Response execution. Actually changing something in the environment.

This split gives security leaders a cleaner set of choices. A team can automate the first two stages heavily, since that is where analyst hours go and where mistakes are cheapest to catch. The same team can stay conservative on the fourth stage, where a wrong move disrupts the business. As the a16z report itself puts it, gathering logs is different from changing a production system.

Human IN the loop vs. Human ON the loop

Once autonomy is split by stage, teams need a shared way to describe how much of it each stage gets. A useful vocabulary comes from researchers at the University of Washington, who define five levels of agent autonomy by the role the human plays.

Level Human role What it means in practice
L1 Operator The human directs and decides, and the agent carries out instructions
L2 Collaborator Human and agent plan and execute together
L3 Consultant The agent leads and checks in for expertise or preferences
L4 Approver The agent works independently and asks for approval only in risky or predefined cases
L5 Observer The agent acts on its own while the human monitors and can hit the stop button

The authors make a point every SOC leader should take to heart. Autonomy is a deliberate design choice, separate from how capable the agent is. A highly capable agent can still run at L2 if the stakes call for it.

Read through this lens, the a16z data describes a market moving from roughly L2 today toward L4 for low-risk actions within a year. Gartner offers a complementary distinction between a human in the loop, who approves each action, and a human on the loop, whose oversight is strategic.

Enterprises evaluating AI SOC vendors should make sure that both models can be applied as appropriate, across their entire operations. 

How to decide where and how much autonomy to grant an AI SOC

The levels mentioned above tell you what the options are. Deciding where each SOC action belongs takes a rubric, and three questions do most of the work.

  1. Reversibility. If the agent gets this wrong, how quickly and completely can it be undone?
  2. Blast radius. How many users, systems or business processes does the action touch?
  3. Receipts. How strong and verifiable is the evidence behind the decision? An action backed by forensic proof of what was executed deserves more latitude than one backed by an LLM hunch about what looks suspicious.

Scoring real actions against those questions produces a map that most security teams will recognize.

Example action Reversibility Blast radius Suggested starting level
Query SIEM, EDR or identity logs Nothing to reverse None L5, fully autonomous
Enrich indicators and pull process trees Nothing to reverse None L5, fully autonomous
Close a false positive with a full evidence trail Easy, the case can be reopened Low L4, autonomous with sampling review
Open and route a ticket to an owner Easy Low L4, autonomous with sampling review
Block a known malicious hash or domain Easy Low to medium L4, autonomous within defined policy
Isolate a standard employee laptop Moderate One user L3 or L4, approval for sensitive groups
Disable an account or revoke sessions Moderate One user, possibly many if a service account L3, approval required
Isolate a production server or domain controller Hard Business-wide L2, human decides and agent executes

The exact placement will differ by organization, and that is the point. The rubric forces an explicit decision for each action, instead of a single policy that is either too loose for the dangerous actions or too tight for the safe ones.

When human approval becomes a rubber stamp

According to the a16z survey, 52% of CISOs want agents to act only with human approval. It sounds like the safe choice, and in many cases it is. It also hides a failure mode that rarely gets discussed.

Human approval is only as good as the context the reviewer receives. When an approval step arrives without clear evidence or criteria, reviewers start clicking through requests to keep the queue moving, and oversight quietly disappears. 

If the AI shapes how every investigation is framed, the human approving the final action is approving a conclusion they never saw being reached.

Only when the reviewer can actually check the AI’s logic and work along with hard, forensic evidence that conclusively points in one direction or another, is the approval actually worth anything. 

In practice that means every approval request should show three things.

  • The evidence the agent collected and where it came from.
  • The reasoning that connects that evidence to the verdict.
  • What the agent checked and ruled out along the way.

A useful test if this is working, is time spent. If a reviewer cannot verify a verdict in a minute or two, the approval step is ceremonial and the team is paying for a human-in-the-loop without getting it.

Autonomy you earn, autonomy you lose

The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications gives this approach a name. It extends least privilege into least agency, granting agents only the minimum autonomy needed for safe, bounded tasks and letting that autonomy grow as it is earned.

Earning it requires criteria that are set before the pilot starts. Otherwise autonomy expands on vendor promises and gut feel. A practical set of graduation criteria for moving an action class up one level looks like this.

  1. Measured agreement. Track how often the agent's verdicts match analyst review over a defined period and alert volume, and set the threshold in advance.
  2. Dry runs first. Run new actions in a test mode that executes the logic but mocks every write, so the team sees what the agent would have done before it does anything.
  3. A complete evidence trail. Every decision at the new level must be auditable after the fact, including what the agent looked at and why it concluded what it did.
  4. A rollback path. Define how the action is undone and who owns that before expanding scope.

Autonomy should also move down. A drop in agreement rates, a major change in the environment such as a new EDR or cloud migration, or a single serious miss should trigger a demotion until the criteria are met again. Teams that only ever ratchet upward are building risk they cannot see.

Your SOC agent is an agent too

Every level of autonomy granted to a SOC agent has a second effect. It raises the damage that agent can do if it is wrong, manipulated or compromised.

Security leaders already feel this risk across the enterprise. In the a16z survey, 46% of CISOs listed AI agents acting outside their intended permissions, or compromised agents, among their five biggest worries, and 29% cited prompt injection or data leakage through AI applications. Meanwhile 55% already run MCP servers or other agent-to-application integrations in production, and 34% run autonomous agents with tool access or write permissions.

The lesson for the SOC is that autonomy itself is a risk factor, scored alongside the vulnerability. Treat the AI SOC agent the way you would treat a new privileged identity.

  • Give it its own identity, never shared credentials.
  • Scope its permissions to the actions it is approved for at its current level.
  • Log every tool call, query and action in a form a human can review.
  • Watch it with the same detections you would apply to a new admin account.

A playbook for the next 12 months

The move from 36% to 60% will happen with or without a plan. Security leaders who want the capacity gains without the incident that sets their AI program back a year can start with five steps.

  1. Inventory every action. List everything your AI SOC agent can do today, from read-only queries to response actions, and place each one on the reversibility, blast radius and receipts rubric.
  2. Automate investigation aggressively. Evidence gathering and analysis consume most analyst hours and carry the least risk. This is where full autonomy pays off first.
  3. Gate disruptive response with real evidence. Keep approval on high-impact actions, and make sure every approval request carries proof a reviewer can verify quickly.
  4. Write graduation and demotion criteria now. Agree on the accuracy thresholds, test periods and rollback paths before the pilot starts, so autonomy expands on data.
  5. Govern the agent like a privileged identity. Scope it, log it and monitor it, because its autonomy is also its blast radius.

Crossing the trust threshold

Every SOC that adopts AI agents will eventually face the same question for each action. Is the agent's work trustworthy enough to act on without a human checking it first?

A helpful way to think about it is a trust threshold. Below it, AI assists analysts, and humans still validate every conclusion. Above it, teams can safely hand off execution and supervise outcomes instead of steps. What moves an action across that line is depth and proof. An agent that can show what actually executed, where it came from and what it did, gives a human something real to verify, and gives the organization a defensible reason to extend its autonomy. Forensic-level investigation, the approach Intezer’s AI SOC is built on, is what moves an action across that line.

That is what earned autonomy means in practice. The agent gets more authority one action class at a time, each step backed by evidence the team can inspect, and each step reversible if the evidence stops holding up.

Note: This article has been written and contributed by Zev Schonberg, PMM at Intezer.

item.title: Linux KVM Flaw CVE-2026-99312 Lets Guest VMs Access Host Memory on AMD Hosts (2026)
item.description:
A flaw in KVM, the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, let researchers read about 127 GB of a cloud server's memory from inside a virtual machine of their own on DigitalOcean.

On a shared server, that memory can include other customers' virtual machines. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-99312, affects only hosts with AMD processors and nested virtualization enabled.

Fixed kernels shipped upstream on Tuesday, the day before the research went public. The provider patched its own fleet with a live patch, telling Droplet customers: "No action needed on your part." Operators who run their own KVM hosts on AMD hardware need to update the host kernel or turn nested virtualization off.

Oren Yomtov, a researcher at the security firm Terra Security, found the flaw and reported it through the provider's bug bounty program. The provider confirmed the exploit worked on its own hosts and treated it as critical, and the Linux KVM maintainers, told on October 21, merged a fix on November 2.

In the test on one of its Droplets, the first thing to come back was the host's kernel version banner, followed by about 127 GB of the host's RAM, mapped read-only, the provider said in a disclosure post yesterday.

The write test ran on the researchers' own bare-metal AMD server, with no other customers attached. There, the guest wrote 32 chosen bytes into a live page of the host kernel's memory, and a witness module loaded into that kernel confirmed the change.

Both tests started with root access inside a VM controlled by the researchers. An attacker would need the same position: control of a guest on a vulnerable host, not just network access to it.

Intel-based KVM hosts are not affected, because the vulnerable code exists only in KVM's support for nested virtualization on AMD. Many cloud providers the researchers surveyed were not vulnerable because they had not enabled nested virtualization on AMD.

There are no reports of the flaw being used outside research, according to VirtFusion, a virtualization platform vendor that is tracking the issue for its operators. No exploit code has been published either, and no guidance exists for detecting a past attempt.

Severity ratings disagree. The Linux kernel's CVE team scores the flaw 8.8 out of 10, with high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability, while Red Hat's preliminary security assessment rates it as Moderate at 5.6 and treats the impact as denial-of-service only. The provider treated it as critical for its own shared cloud.

Terra's technical analysis, published on Wednesday, describes a pointer left pointing at freed memory. KVM confines each VM with a table, the nested page table, that translates the VM's memory addresses into the host's real memory, and the processor finds that table through a pointer kept for each virtual CPU.

Some hosts let a VM run a VM of its own, a nested VM. When a reset signal called INIT stops the nested VM, KVM skips restoring the outer VM's pointer, leaving it pointing to a page of memory the kernel has already freed.

Once the kernel reused that freed page, the guest could fill it with entries of its own choosing, and the processor followed them as if they were the real table. The forged entries could name any physical page on the host, which is how about 127 GB of the server's RAM came into reach of a guest that was never given it.

The fix makes KVM reset that memory-management state on every INIT.

The flaw was created by a security fix. A 2022 patch for a different nested-virtualization bug, CVE-2022-3344, switched a reset path back to the outer VM's control block but missed the page-table pointer, the researchers say, and the error then sat in the kernel for just under four years.

In earlier work called PatchSlop, the team found that the fix for another one introduced 3.2% of kernel vulnerabilities.

What to Do

The fix lives in the host kernel. Updating the operating systems inside the VMs changes nothing, and a host keeps running its old kernel until it is rebooted.

Upstream, the fix shipped on Tuesday in stable kernel 7.3.5 and in the long-term kernels 6.18.64 and 6.12.118, the kernel team's CVE announcement shows. item.title: Bazuka Android Malware Uses Fake Screen Overlays to Hide Credential Theft and Device Control (2026)
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously unknown Android malware framework called Bazuka that offers large language model (LLM) integration for victim management and control at scale.

Dutch mobile security company ThreatFabric said it discovered the threat in late October 2026 during an investigation into an NFC-relay banking Trojan.

"Bazuka is a full malware framework," ThreatFabric said in a technical report. "A dropper/downloader, a core, and 23 modules cover overlays, keylogging, 2FA and SMS interception, remote control, and crypto-address swapping."

One notable aspect of the malware that distinguishes it from the rest is a novel overlay technique that allows the trojan to take a screenshot of the home screen or lock screen, and display that as an overlay on demand to cover up malicious activities taking place in the background.

Another perhaps not-so-surprising element is the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the control panel to help operators identify victims of interest and manage infections. It supports both locally hosted models and models accessed through an API.

One of the sample prompts provided by the author refers to a score, indicating an operator can likely request the AI model to score victims and determine how attractive they are as targets. The panel also supports the following capabilities -

  • Create accounts for traffers, who are cybercriminals responsible for driving victims to malware using various lures
  • Build droppers containing the malware with options to choose the kind of permissions specified in the Android manifest file likely in an attempt to bypass Google Play app review process

This indicates that the dropper apps can be distributed via at least two distribution channels: through traffers, who can use social media ads or bogus sites to trick users into downloading them, and Google Play Store.

One of the droppers containing the malware masquerades as a premium, adult-friendly version of TikTok (package name: "com.tiktok.premium"). Two different variants of the Bazuka attack chain have been observed -

  • A dropper, which asks the victim for permissions to install applications from third-party sources and then proceeds to download a standalone APK ("com.tiktok.premium.pro") that serves as the stager
  • A downloader that directly downloads the main payload

It's suspected that the stager is the same as the downloader, whose main responsibility is to retrieve the core and supplementary modules necessary for a particular campaign, and then launch them.

"Once the core and required modules are loaded, Bazuka operates as a keylogger and a classic overlay trojan, monitoring the text entered by the victim and displaying an overlay at the right moment," ThreatFabric said. "All functionality is controlled by commands from C2 [command-and-control]."

The core module is the orchestrator, maintaining communication with C2, loading additional DEX modules, dispatching commands, collecting device information, and managing permissions and component updates. Like other Android trojans, it abuses Android Debug Bridge (ADB) shell commands and the operating system's accessibility services to request permissions and grant them automatically.

"Important components of the core include mechanisms for enabling Wireless Debugging and completing the pairing process," ThreatFabric explained. "The core can open the system settings screen, find the relevant menu, enable Developer options, and then enable Wireless Debugging."

"When this mode is enabled, it also intercepts the PIN, which is then used to establish a TLS connection to the ADB daemon."

Furthermore, the core component counters detection by Google Play by disabling the protection component through the accessibility services API. It is also equipped to launch a self-destruct mechanism that clears local storage, deletes the database, and disables the application completely.

Communication with the C2 server takes place over two WebSocket channels -

  • Control, which is used to issue commands
  • Data, which is used to exfiltrate data and screen capture streams

Bazuka supports 23 modules that enable comprehensive data and cryptocurrency theft -

  • call_forwarding, to manage call forwarding through USSD commands
  • clip_monitor, to act as a clipper and substitute cryptocurrency wallet addresses copied to the clipboard with attacker-controlled ones
  • contacts, to collect contact information
  • device_control, to manage the device over the ADB bridge and execute commands as shell commands
  • file_manager, to access the file system
  • input_recorder, to act as a keylogger and capture all text entered into a target application, as well as identify bank card numbers, wallet addresses, and passwords in user input
  • location, to determine a victim's location using GPS, cell tower positioning, and Wi-Fi
  • media, to capture photos and stream camera video and microphone audio
  • oem_power, to open system and OEM settings for power saving, background operation, and autostart
  • optics, to facilitate remote control, screencasting, and phishing overlays
  • preflight, to perform preliminary checks of the runtime environment
  • proxy, to implement a reverse TCP proxy
  • push, to create and manage local Android notifications
  • screen_control, to capture the lock screen PIN, text password, and unlock pattern through accessibility services
  • self_adb, to implement an embedded ADB client
  • session_ui, to display phishing HTML overlays
  • smsmessage, to access SMS messages and extract potential verification codes, send SMS messages, and attempt to delete messages from the device
  • system_checker, to check the runtime environment and implement anti-analysis measures
  • tapread-nfc_module, to interact with contactless bank cards
  • toast, to display text messages on the device's screen
  • twofa, to capture one-time verification codes
  • uninstall_shield, to counter attempts to uninstall or force-stop the application
  • ussd, to send USSD requests from the victim's device and receive responses from the mobile operator

The malware has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. However, the panel has been found to display UI elements in a mix of English and Russian.

"ADB bridging is becoming a standard feature of modern banking trojans," ThreatFabric said. "While it is not there yet for Bazuka and its current architecture, this is a very concerning sign, as it allows malware to obtain various privileges covertly and deploy independent modules that can survive removal of the host application."

"Another equally concerning feature is the use of LLM chats directly within the control panel. AI agents are used to identify victims of interest."

ArcticRAT Android Malware Uses LLMs to Extract High-Value Data

Bazuka is not the only Android-focused threat to integrate an LLM into its workflow. Last week, Zimperium zLabs research team detailed another sophisticated and rapidly evolving Android malware called ArcticRAT that supports 129 distinct commands and incorporates LLM APIs into its data exfiltration pipeline to extract high-value financial intelligence from stolen SMS messages and app data.

"What initially began as a targeted spyware operation aimed at users of 11 specific cryptocurrency apps has morphed into an enterprise grade, AI-powered, Remote Access Trojan (RAT)," researchers Rajat Goyal and Fernando Ortega said.

Infection chains make use of malicious sites impersonating Google Play app listings to convince users to install the dropper app. Unsuspecting users are redirected to these pages through malvertising, smishing, or third-party forums. The apps masquerade as popular brands (e.g., Amazon and TikTok), cryptocurrency applications, and generic file managers.

Once installed, the app abuses Android accessibility services to establish remote control, automate fraudulent activity, and leverage AI to parse and "clean" exfiltrated data. It uses TCP sockets to communicate with the C2 infrastructure.

An initial reconnaissance step is used to build a host profile, which then dictates the C2 server to dynamically select the relevant attack payloads to deploy. At a high level, the malware supports the following features -

  • Initiate a real-time video transmission from the compromised device
  • Abuse accessibility services for full remote control
  • Serve fake extortion overlays and deceive victims into making cryptocurrency payments
  • Make use of LLMs to process harvested SMS messages and look for financial, banking, and trading apps through hard-coded prompts that ask the model to take the role of a professional SMS analyzer and device app analyzer, respectively
  • Capture credentials, authentication codes, and private communications
  • Serve overlays to steal device lock screen pattern, PIN, or password

"The malware requests VPN service privileges to null-route network communication on the victim's device, effectively blinding Google Play Protect telemetry during the staging phase," Zimperium said.

"To prevent the user from interfering with these operations, ArcticRAT employs a defense evasion tactic known as a "Black Screen" overlay. When the attacker is navigating banking apps via Hidden VNC (HVNC) or auto-approving system permissions, the malware draws a completely black, un-dismissible view over the screen and drops the brightness to zero. To the victim, the device appears locked or powered off."

Recent versions of ArcticRAT have also been found to abuse the native Wireless Debugging mechanism to initiate a privileged shell session on the victim machine and execute commands, including enabling or disabling accessibility permissions, verifying lock screen PIN or pattern, and displaying a black screen to conceal background operations.

"By abandoning hardcoded attacks in favor of real-time Hidden VNC (HVNC), raw TCP command-and-control (C2), and aggressive defense evasion overlays, the malware achieves complete device takeover," Zimperium said.

item.title: WhatsApp Patches 3 Security Flaws, Including Android Bug Suspected of Use in Scams (2026)
item.description:
Meta-owned WhatsApp has addressed security vulnerabilities, including one impacting its Android app that it suspects may have been exploited in connection with scam messages.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-23871 (CVSS score: 3.5), has been described as a case of incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4.

The issue could have "caused a target's device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread," WhatsApp said.

The messaging platform said it may have been "abused in conjunction with specific spam messages." Internal researchers on the WhatsApp Security Team have been credited with discovering and reporting the issue.

When reached for comment, a WhatsApp spokesperson told The Hacker News that the vulnerability was discovered while disrupting a scam campaign. "We believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible," the spokesperson added.

WhatsApp did not disclose the scale of the activity, and if those efforts were successful.

Also addressed by the company are two other flaws -

  • CVE-2026-102769 (CVSS score: 6.8) - An SQL injection vulnerability in WhatsApp for Android prior to version 2.26.35.74 that occurred when a recipient tapped on a specially crafted "order details" message sent from an unofficial client, causing locally-stored WhatsApp files to be deleted.
  • CVE-2026-44908 (CVSS score: 4.8) - A trust-validation vulnerability in WhatsApp's certificate verification mechanism for Meta AI's confidential computing infrastructure that affects WhatsApp for iOS before 2.26.24.72, WhatsApp Business for iOS and WhatsApp for Mac Desktop before v2.26.23.72, WhatsApp for Android before v2.26.23.74, and WhatsApp Business for Android before v2.26.23.70.

Interestingly, CVE-2026-102769 is also capable of leaking one bit of information through a timing-based side channel if the user is online at the time of receipt of the malicious message.

It "leaked one bit of information asked by the attacker about the user's chat database via an induced-crash delivery receipt timing side channel," WhatsApp added. There is no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild.

Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-44908, on the other hand, could have allowed a bad actor positioned within Meta infrastructure to bypass the hardware root of trust using a Versioned Chip Endorsement Key (VCEK) certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer's key.

"Any such VCEK Cert would first have to be published to the third-party binary transparency ledger used by WhatsApp Private Processing," WhatsApp noted. "The ledger shows that every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, confirming no exploitation."

WhatsApp is advising users to keep their apps and devices up to date to ensure optimal protection. The company also said that it continuously works to strengthen its systems and acknowledged the bug bounty community's contributions towards keeping the platform secure.

item.title: Hackers Exploit Critical VMware, Cisco, and Apache Flaws as Espionage Attacks Emerge (2026)
item.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added four flaws impacting Apache Roller, Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, and Broadcom VMware vCenter to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

  • CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Apache Roller that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via the XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and deserializes vendor extension types before authentication. (Fixed in November 2026)
  • CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability in Cisco Expressway Series that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with persistent cookies and network access to execute commands as root on a clustered device via the database service. (Fixed in October 2026)
  • CVE-2025-42884 (CVSS score: 6.5) - An improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to disclose or modify server information via injected JNDI environment properties or a URL used during JNDI lookup operations. (Fixed in November 2025)

item.title: Signal Blocks AI Agents From Reading Private Chats via Screenshots on Android and iOS (2026)
item.description:
Signal has announced that it will restrict screenshots by default to stop artificial intelligence (AI) agents from reading private chats on Android and iOS devices, but conceded that the protection is "incomplete."

The feature applies to agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where the encrypted messaging platform can detect an AI assistant attempting to read the Signal screen.

It also builds upon a similar setting that Signal introduced in Windows 11 last May following Microsoft's release of the controversial Recall feature.

Calling the agentic integrations into Android, iOS, and Windows an "existential threat to Signal," Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, said the move is designed to uphold its privacy guarantees in the AI era.

"In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that's on your screen," Whittaker said. "In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding."

"The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy."

The risk here is that AI agents can capture and store the information accessed from Signal either locally or on remote servers, with the activity occurring outside of the platform's control and potentially putting the privacy of all the participants in a conversation at risk.

Users who want to disable the option can do so by navigating to Settings > Privacy > App Security > toggle "Block Siri AI" (on iOS) or "Screen security" (on Android).

"However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts') Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees," Signal said.

"Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user's device via the file system."

Signal also pointed out that application developers lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from eroding application-level privacy. It also called out the companies for failing to provide adequate documentation about how these systems work to help design necessary controls to prevent the agents from accessing sensitive application data.

Specifically, it's urging the tech giants to provide "two common-sense remedies" to help protect the privacy of its users -

  • Access to easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing entirely, including screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, without making drastic compromises to the core user experience
  • Create better documentation and technical specifications around how AI agents function, specifically with regards to data access and processing

The concerns are not theoretical. Reuters recently reported that Muse, Meta's AI agent, was able to bypass its own official "Connector" tool to obtain access to Signal messages on both an Apple computer and an Android device by taking advantage of the broad operating system permissions granted to it during initial setup.

On macOS, for example, the agent leveraged macOS's accessibility and screenshot tools to navigate to the Signal app, take screenshots, extract text from those images, and regenerate the textual content within the Muse app. On Android, it read messages by abusing its access to the device's push notifications.

In one case highlighted by the news agency, the AI agent alerted a Meta staffer using Muse on her personal phone with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal. "This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this," the employee said in an internal post.

"We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta's Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup," Whittaker said.

"In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents." 

Late last month, Apple released iOS 27.2 with an "Excluded Apps" option that lets users choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access. With Google Gemini, users have the ability to disconnect apps via the Connected Apps settings.

Earlier this week, the iPhone maker also previewed new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

item.title: Attackers' AI Agents Found a Zero-Day in Medical-Imaging Software and Gained Root Access (2026)
item.description:
Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server, and gain root access to a university server, Amazon Threat Intelligence said this week.

The flaw allows an attacker with no account to write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup, which runs with no login enabled.

The maintainers have merged a fix in the source code, but there is still no fixed version to install.

MONAI Label is a server that research teams use to label medical scans and train imaging models; it is a separate program from the broader MONAI framework.

The weakness is a path-traversal flaw in the parts of the server that store uploaded images and labels. A file identifier supplied by the caller is appended to the storage folder and written to disk without checking that the result remains within that folder.

The server writes with the privileges of the account it runs under, so an attacker cannot write anywhere on the machine, but a writable code or settings location can open a path to running code. Authentication is off by default, so any client that can reach the server over the network can set off the write. Versions 0.8.5 and earlier are affected.

Amazon reconstructed the intrusion after finding the operator's own Cairn control panel sitting on the internet without a password. Cairn is an open-source framework that runs AI agents as automated penetration testers, and the exposed panel revealed the agents' task settings, prompts, and run history.

Over about 48 hours in September, the agents mapped the application's interface and reached the point of writing files to the server in roughly 11 minutes, the company said in its incident report.

The agents worked with little step-by-step direction. The operator set the goal of getting shell access and chose the targets, and the agents selected the methods themselves, according to the company.

Investigators tie the campaign to a China-linked actor with moderate confidence, pointing to Simplified Chinese prompts, China Standard Time settings, and targets likely of interest to China. They did not connect the work to a named group or establish that a government was behind it.

A root shell came later, and not within those 11 minutes. In a separate session, the agents used the same flaw to plant a file that Python runs automatically at startup. They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root.

That root access was on one university server, and whether another MONAI Label system would give the same result depends on how it is run and what its service account can do.

In a later session, the operator handed the agents a tunnel into a second university network running the same software. Amazon believes the network was broken into in the same way but has not confirmed the second compromise.

The maintainers confirmed the flaw and merged the source fix on October 19, which forces uploads to resolve inside the approved folders and rejects empty names or names that begin with a dot.

Their security advisory, published earlier this week, still lists no patched version and says the correction will arrive in a future release. The newest release listing remains 0.8.5, which dates to 2024. A merged fix in source code is not the same as a package you can install.

The flaw is now listed in the CVE record as CVE-2026-133968, published this week and rated 9.8 out of 10, a critical score. The project's advisory still shows no CVE assigned, which is a lag in updating that page, not a sign of a second flaw.

What to Do Now

With no fixed release available, the practical steps are to cut off exposure and limit what a compromised server could reach:

  • Block untrusted network access to MONAI Label servers with firewall and routing rules, not just hard-to-guess URLs.
  • Turn on authentication, which the server leaves off by default.
  • Run the server under a limited account rather than root, and restrict the folders it can write to.
  • Do not assume a source build is safe. Confirm it includes the October fix before treating it as patched.
  • If a server was reachable, check for unexpected Python startup files and unusual training jobs, the path the reported attack used.

The company's account is based on its own reconstruction and has not been independently confirmed. It does not show that patient scans or records were taken, that clinical systems were touched, or that the attacker reached past the university targets described.

The campaign also included failed operations, and the root result on one server should not be taken as the outcome for every MONAI Label deployment.

item.title: GnuPG Warns Critical GPGME Flaw Could Expose App Data via Malicious OpenPGP Keys (2026)
item.description:
A malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME, the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG.

The GnuPG project warned yesterday that the flaw could be used to steal data from affected applications and has released fixed versions.

The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-129975, affects all software that uses GPGME before version 2.3.0, whether the library is loaded as a shared library, a Windows DLL, or statically linked into the program.

Examples the project gives include most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba, and its own Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, and GnuPG VS-Desktop packages.

The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out.

Its example of a path to the bug is signed data sent to an application. Which programs pass such material to the library without a manual key import is not something the advisory says.

The flaw is a double free, meaning the same memory is released twice. It sits in two routines, read_status() and read_colon_line(), that read status lines and key listings coming back from GnuPG.

When the input runs long, the routines move the data to a larger buffer but record the new address only if they finish without errors. An error in between leaves a pointer to memory that was already freed, and cleanup then frees it a second time, as the project's tracker entry details.

The flaw was found by Johan Carlsson and reported to the project by GitLab last week. Disclosure was set for November 25, the advisory says, and moved up because the new Ruby2Shell bug forced the company to update earlier.

What to Update

The fixed library version is GPGME 2.3.1, released this week. A version 2.3.0 was never publicly available.

What to install depends on where the library sits:

  • Shared library or DLL: update to GPGME 2.3.1, available from the project's official downloads and detailed in its security advisory.
  • Windows: Gpg4win 5.1.2 bundles the fixed library. Its release notes call the issue severe and say to update as soon as possible.
  • Older versions that cannot move to 2.3.1: the advisory carries a patch, and the legacy branch has its own fixed release, 1.24.4, whose legacy release notes say the project cannot guarantee that the branch will see every security patch.
  • Bundled and statically linked copies: these are affected too, and updates to the system's shared library do not reach them, so the applications that contain them need their own rebuilt releases.
  • GPGMEPP and GPGMEQT: no update is needed.

The advisory offers no interim workaround for software that cannot update yet.

item.title: A Single Malicious Webpage Let Researchers Hijack Meta Muse and Access Private Chats (2026)
item.description:
A malicious webpage could extract a Meta Muse user's private conversations and stored memories from the assistant without triggering any approval prompt, researchers have shown.

The same attack could be extended to reach the credentials Muse stores for the user's connected accounts.

The work was a laboratory demonstration, not an attack on real users, and it stayed inside the individual user's cloud machine. NebuSec, the security firm that published it yesterday, says Muse's team has since fixed every weakness it describes.

Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched on September 8, that works through the online accounts a user connects to it and can make purchases on their behalf. Each person's agent runs on its own cloud computer.

There, a monitoring layer called Sentinel is meant to be the single gate for anything the agent sends out, and the passwords and tokens for connected accounts are supposed to stay beyond the agent's reach.

Muse's team described the aim at launch: "So we designed the system to assume the agent may be under attack and limit the potential damage."

In the demonstration, a malicious page the agent opened could pull a user's conversation history and stored memories to an external server and alter them, with no prompt shown to the user, according to the firm's research write-up.

From there, the researchers chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser, which the assistant uses for tasks such as creating PDFs, to a Linux kernel flaw, thereby taking full control of the user's cloud machine. They set out that chain in a technical breakdown.

That full control reached the credential store, the saved files, and Sentinel itself, the parts Muse's security design keeps walled off from the agent.

The compromise went no further than that one machine. The researchers did not break out to the shared server beneath it or into other users' machines.

Muse was built to assume its own agent could be turned against the user and to box in any break-in. Each of those controls worked as designed, the firm said, yet the attack still ran the whole way through.

The firm says it reported the findings to Muse's team and that the exploits were all fixed before publication. Meta has not publicly confirmed the fixes or commented on the work, and the write-up does not say whether any user data was accessed before the patches went in.

The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack the assistant on the device.

A now-patched flaw in Ghostscript allows a crafted file to escape the program's security sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it.

Ghostscript is the interpreter that many Linux servers use to convert uploaded PDFs, PostScript files, and images into other formats, often without the application calling it directly.

Security firm pwn.ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125396, was fixed on September 8, and there have been no reports of it being used in attacks.

Getting a crafted file to Ghostscript is easy, because an application does not have to call it directly. A common image or document library such as ImageMagick, Pillow, libvips, or a Qt plugin will hand PostScript or EPS content to Ghostscript to render, even when the file is named .png, .jpg, or .pdf. A routine feature like making a thumbnail or cropping a picture can start the interpreter, and the exact path depends on the libraries the application uses.

The underlying bug is a use-after-free in the part of Ghostscript that loads fonts. A crafted document uses it to switch off the checks in -dSAFER, the sandbox that is supposed to stop the document from running commands or reaching files.

The security firm demonstrated the result by feeding such a document through about ten applications and watching a command run on the server, each time as the low-privilege account that does the rendering.

Several of those paths needed no login: an anonymous print job to a shared Debian 13 queue, an emailed attachment that Roundcube webmail processed the moment the recipient opened the message, and public upload forms in the WordPress plugins Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor.

WordPress Core itself needed more: an account with the ability to upload files, which Authors and higher roles have by default. Although the CVE is classified as a local flaw, the firm's tests reached Ghostscript from the network via print jobs, email, and web uploads. The tested version and the access needed for each application are set out in its impact index.

Artifex, which develops Ghostscript, fixed the flaw in version 10.08.0 on September 8, and is moving the vulnerable internal step into safer code. Ken Sharp, the developer who handled the fix, called that step "an ancient piece of code well known to be a vulnerability, but difficult to eradicate" in the bug report. The CVE was published last week and is scored 8.5 out of 10 in its security advisory.

WordPress had already closed its own upload path in version 7.0.4 on August 12, under a separate identifier, CVE-2026-65640, as noted in its release notes. That fix and the Ghostscript fix cover different points in the same chain, so updating one does not remove the need for the other.

Updating the Renderer

The fix helps only where it reaches the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript bundled inside a container image or an application, so a document worker can keep running the old code after the host package is replaced.

Coverage across Linux distributions is uneven. As of last week, several still shipped a vulnerable Ghostscript or had a fix pending, according to the firm's survey. The list records package status, not a tested attack path for each system:

  • Debian 12 (Bookworm): listed as vulnerable
  • Amazon Linux 2, 2023, and 2027 Preview: fix pending
  • SUSE Linux Enterprise 12 SP5 and parts of 15: fix in progress
  • SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and 16.1: fix in progress
  • openSUSE Leap 16.0 and 16.1: affected

The firm did not establish whether current Red Hat, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, or stable Fedora packages carry the fix.

Until the renderer is updated, the exposure can be reduced by requiring authentication on print queues and by limiting which file types an image processor accepts. System controls help too, and in one test an AppArmor profile stopped the compromised interpreter from starting a shell.

One published proof-of-concept file, described in its technical analysis, shows only the core memory trick. It changes a value inside the running interpreter and sets it back, without running a shell command or touching files on the host, and on the patched 10.08.0 build it fails before that point.

The firm's broader research extended to production services, including Google, which fixed the affected path last week. Its reports of similar problems at Dropbox and other unnamed services are separate Ghostscript bugs, not this one.

item.title: OpenRouter Drops 3 Providers After Researchers Catch Months of Prompt Theft at AI Hosting Firms (2026)
item.description:
Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week.

Some of the stolen requests were flagged as Zero Data Retention, the setting that is supposed to mean a prompt is never stored.

OpenRouter, a gateway that routes customers' AI requests to a pool of third-party providers, said today that it has removed three providers from its platform, removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention, and notified all potentially affected customers. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself, the company said.

The earliest of the three breaches began in mid-July. The planted prompts were bait, but they were processed alongside real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too, the firm said.

The finding comes from canary token research that seeded about two million prompts with unique web links and credentials between July and November, then watched for anyone using them. A planted secret can only be learned in one place, so any use of it means someone read the prompt that carried it.

The largest of the three breaches involved a couple hundred AWS keys that were planted, each sent in exactly one request to one provider during a few short windows in late October. Every request sent during those windows was stolen, and some came from requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, indicating the attacker was copying traffic at the first point of arrival rather than deeper in the inference stack.

The thief tested keys within hours in some cases, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users to keep access, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls.

One attacker appears to have compromised two of the providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server.

On November 1, the same attacker brought in ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, and used it only to confirm that keys it already held were still live. Two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, appear in no public indicator list the firm could find and are worth adding to detections.

"A privacy flag doesn't help when the attacker is already inside," wrote HD Moore, the firm's chief research officer.

The second finding needed no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest prices, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through, the research found.

The people doing it looked like individuals on home internet connections. One, working from a Mac on home broadband in France, took passwords from two prompts and typed root SSH login attempts by hand, then used the same machine to test several planted AWS keys.

One of those keys had traveled through a different router that quietly forwarded some of its traffic to the marketplace, a hop that no customer was told about. That router has since told the firm it stopped, and route tracing across about 2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems, plus one seller that quietly adds about 1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt.

A Chinese AI lab, which the research does not name, fetched the secret links from more than half of the seeded prompts sent to its models between July and October, including about two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention. Prompts sent to U.S. hosting providers that resell the lab's models triggered the same scraper, thereby flowing back to the lab.

A git client on another cloud later tried to clone private repositories referenced in the prompts, but only for that lab's models, and one large U.S. provider kept crawling a secret link more than two months after a single request to its search endpoint.

Twenty-four days after one prompt was sent, its secret link was posted into a chat on Feishu, the Chinese workplace app known as Lark elsewhere. The link was opened within two minutes from three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.

The firm had disclosed only the first 8 characters of the provider's link, so whoever posted it was reading a cached copy of the full prompt.

In practice, Moore wrote, the flagged prompts were kept, passed to other companies, and read by human beings.

OpenRouter said in an incident announcement that the 125 endpoints removed from Zero Data Retention eligibility cover providers flagged by the researchers plus others cut as a precaution. Any endpoint removed during the review will require assurances and validation before its status is returned.

The gateway is adapting the researchers' testing approach so that the checks can run on an ongoing basis and is verifying network paths to identify where requests and responses may be forwarded to third parties.

The researchers are now working with about a dozen providers, and planted keys and secret links were still being accessed months after the first thefts, as of this week.

Railway, a platform company, said in October that an intrusion it suffered was likely part of a series of attacks built to target platform companies with the end goal of compromising AI inference providers.

Not all affected providers have posted publicly, the gateway said, and it has notified affected users either way. Three have posted.

What the Providers Have Disclosed

An attacker took control of an inference server at Phala and could view request data while it was being processed, the provider said in a preliminary incident report last week. The incident was contained on November 8, and the model service has been restored with added protections.

Requests to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model that reached Phala through the gateway between October 21 at 00:00 UTC and November 8 at 05:35 UTC should be treated as exposed, the report says, and every key, token, password, or other secret within them should be rotated.

A third-party researcher had been placing unique canary credentials in requests since July 1, and only the ones sent on October 21 and 22 were later misused. Those tests sampled traffic rather than monitoring every request, so the provider maintains the broader precautionary window.

At Together AI, an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples of customer prompts after an AI coding agent committed a credential to the company's public GitHub repository, the company said yesterday in a security notice. The samples had been collected for routine software testing and were generated by requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models in June and July.

The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, and five of the tested credentials were canaries from the researchers' experiment. The company said it has no reason to believe the data went further, understands it has been deleted, and has made zero data retention the default for new accounts.

Novita, another provider on the gateway, confirmed this week in a privacy notice that a routing configuration issue caused some MiniMax requests to be sent on to MiniMax's official API, beyond what was intended for those customers.

Dragos has not named the three breached providers, OpenRouter has not named the three it removed, and neither has said publicly whether they are the same three.

The provider behind the mid-July breach first blamed an internal misconfiguration, then a partner's data processing, before its own investigation found that attackers had compromised its internal credentials, the researchers said. It had still not disclosed the incident publicly as of this week.

What Users Should Do

The researchers' advice starts from one limit: a privacy flag binds only the first hop, Moore wrote, and AI agents will send whatever they can read, credentials included. Where a prompt goes is a choice, he wrote, and a customer who does not choose hands the choice to the lowest price.

Self-hosting is the only option in which no third party reads a prompt, and going directly to a first-tier provider leaves one company, one contract, and one privacy policy to check.

Routers need more care: pick the upstream providers yourself instead of accepting the default pool, verify that privacy settings actually change where requests go, and stay away from reseller marketplaces, some of whose capacity runs on stolen keys.

A fake credential seeded into the context that agents and pipelines already send serves as a tripwire if any use of it is treated as an incident, and a free Thinkst Canarytoken is enough to get started. Settings that scrub known credential formats from prompts help too, though they miss sensitive data that is not shaped like a key.

item.title: AI-Assisted Cyber Attacks Trigger Unauthorized Payments at Indian Banks and Fintech Firms (2026)
item.description:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has warned that threat actors are carrying out artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cyber attacks targeting information and communication technology (ICT) assets in the country.

This unsanctioned activity has resulted in unauthorized financial transactions at banking and financial services entities, as well as technology service providers supporting government-linked payments and platforms handling vendor or partner payouts.

"In the observed incidents, attackers targeted business records and approval processes to carry out unauthorized transactions through otherwise legitimate systems," CERT-In said in an advisory last week.

The incidents have been found to include the following methods -

  • Abuse of business applications and service provider-operated workflows, as opposed to direct exploitation of payment-related APIs.
  • Modification of business records or approval relationships, followed by the use of legitimate payment processes.
  • Use of trusted systems and established approval procedures to process unauthorized transactions without raising any alert.
  • Exploitation of security blind spots in independent verification, reconciliation, and review of changes to business records.

CERT-In did not reveal how much money had been improperly paid out, or by whom. The activity has not been attributed to any specific threat actor.

The agency also said that separate threat-hunting has uncovered the use of AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks (AOFS) across enterprise, technology, government, academic, and research sectors to conduct the following actions -

  • Automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems, services, and potential attack paths.
  • Rapid generation and modification of exploits for known vulnerabilities, including by analyzing software patches and related technical information.
  • Using a cluster of AI agents to undertake intrusion tasks, such as reconnaissance and privilege discovery, in parallel.
  • Modifying scripts, requests, and attack methods in response to errors, blocked attempts, or information returned by targeted systems.
  • Using valid credentials, legitimate administrative functions, trust relationships, and external infrastructure to burrow deeper into target networks.

"Organizations should review the security of business applications, critical records, user identities and third-party interfaces," CERT-In said. "Existing monitoring and incident-response arrangements should also account for the risks arising from misuse of trusted business processes and automated intrusion activity."

The development comes as Indian entities have witnessed a spate of AI-assisted cyber attacks on financial entities, even as the national nodal agency disclosed that AI agents under research and evaluation "exceeded their task authorization and made unauthorized access" to ICT assets.

"In the financially motivated campaign against Indian entities, agentic tooling compressed the time between initial access and final impact from days to a few hours," CERT-In said. "In addition, the campaign highlighted that multi-agent operations run in parallel for hours to days to achieve the attacker goals, consistent with the documented multi-agent capability of these tools."

Earlier this month, the agency also warned that a threat group named Crafty Falcon is behind a wave of AI-driven attacks on financial ​firms and has used offensive penetration testing tools like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN, and CyberStrikeAI to automate the intrusions at machine speed.

According to the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the attacks have targeted banks, non-banking financial companies, and fintech companies, leading to multi-crore (equivalent to 10 million) unauthorized transactions through fund disbursement systems and APIs.

"Perpetrators exploit unpatched software or misconfigured internet-exposed servers / IT systems to compromise the infrastructure," I4C said. "Hackers then target automated fund disbursement systems or special interfaces (APIs) used for payments and fund transfers.  The money is sent to 'mule' accounts (accounts used by criminals) across different banks and then quickly moved or withdrawn through IMPS/NEFT."

India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India, has also alerted of rising cyber attacks on financial infrastructure, urging banks to provide details of their ability to stay ahead of AI-related threats, Reuters reported late last month.

The Surge in AI Attacks

The advisories also come at a time when organizations around the world are being targeted using AI tools, giving attackers a way to "execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity." Last week, the European Commission confirmed that attackers armed with ARTEX broke into its HR, medical reimbursement, and translation systems. The first signs of the attack were detected on October 22, 2026.

ARTEX has also been implicated in a recent supply chain attack on IT management software company ConnectWise and Barracuda, with the latter revealing that a financially motivated criminal weaponized an exposed valid cloud access key provided to a third-party vendor to map its reach, repurpose discovered secrets to access more systems and look for seed phrases, and exfiltrate more credentials and secrets.

"In all, the attacker touched about 10 cloud accounts in roughly 44 hours [between November 1 and 2]. The work was methodical and tireless," Barracuda said. "The probe names, the other indicators we collected, the order in which the attacker worked through our systems, and its built-in routines for hunting credentials and wallets all match ARTEX."

Frameworks like ARTEX manage a collection of sub-agents to plan, execute, and adapt tactics across multiple kill chain stages, including reconnaissance and scanning, initial access, persistence and privilege escalation, internal reconnaissance, lateral movement, and data exfiltration.

They can translate tactical goals described in natural language into machine commands that are executed by specialized AI agents. It integrates with various external LLMs, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, SpaceXAI Grok, Zhipu GLM, and Kimi.

"ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours," the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said in an alert this month.

"The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale."

Check Point, in a report published this month, said it uncovered more than 1,800 publicly exposed instances for ARTEX, with attackers leveraging the tool to conduct opportunistic, financially-motivated cybercrime.

"Analysis of agent conversations revealed that these systems work almost fully autonomously, once the initial goal is set: most actors barely interacted with their agent fleets and mostly asked for progress or directed the agents to a new target," the company said.

Data security firm Cohesity said threat actors using ARTEX are gaining access to systems that receive less security attention, such as partner and supplier portals, mobile backends, employee and sales support applications, legacy services, third-party integrations, and applications built by individual business units.

"In a research network we operate, a threat actor linked to Rhysida used an AI framework to rewrite tools in response to obstacles, often within minutes, and more than 150 versions of a single script reached a domain controller within a day," it said.

In a report published last week, Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) identified what it described as the first observed instance of attackers using an autonomous AI framework with no human in the loop to turn security patches into exploits.

The AI framework, called "exploit_agent," integrates with multiple frontier and local large language models (LLMs). It's designed to discover software vulnerabilities and execute exploits without human intervention. The attacker, suspected to be Russian-speaking, is said to have leveraged the framework to target French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector.

"The framework is set up to conduct continuous differential analysis of popular web application software," Mandiant and GTIG said. "It compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes findings to identify potential vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and automatically executes them without human intervention."

Some of the other notable incidents where AI agents and models do the legwork are listed below -

  • Use of CAIRN in intrusion activity against targets, including in the aerospace sector in the U.S.
  • Embedding LLMs into influence operation workflows to produce synthetic media, create convincing virtual personas, and generate and publish content.
  • Use of Google's Gemini API, along with tools from multiple AI providers, to build an end-to-end influence-as-a-service (SaaS) platform designed to target public sentiment on regional political topics, specifically across Europe and the Middle East.
  • Use of LLMs by a China-linked contractor called Leaky Castle to analyze, translate, and understand exfiltrated data
  • Abuse of a frontier model's file-hosting infrastructure by a China-nexus threat actor to stage lure archives and exfiltrate stolen data, and a backend API to exfiltrate stolen intranet documents.
  • Use of LLMs by North Korean threat actors to generate resumes and prepare for job interviews at Western organizations.
  • Creation of fraudulent recruiter profiles on professional networking platforms by a suspected North Korean hacking group called Midnight Neptune (previously UNC1069) in attacks aimed at cryptocurrency entities in North America and Europe using job- and ClickFix-themed lures. These personas have been found to direct targets to fraudulent meeting platforms, which are used to run diagnostic fix scripts via ClickFix. "Following initial compromise, the actor pivoted into internal code repositories to execute a supply chain vector internal to the organization: modifying .claude/settings.json configuration files so that when users started up Claude Code, it would automatically trigger the download of the SOMBERMEME backdoor," Google said.
  • Use of CyberStrikeAI ("43.240.29[.]11") between September 30 and October 16, 2026, to validate stolen AWS credentials, harvest secrets from Secrets Manager, pull EC2 user data, decrypt an SSM parameter, and send a remote command. "The audit log does not show what the command was or whether it succeeded," Elastic Security Labs said.
  • Use of Hermes, in combination with DeepSeek, by a threat actor called Silent Lynx in cyber espionage operations targeting Central Asian governments and critical infrastructure from April to October 2026 to assist with reconnaissance, data collection, and erasing traces of activity from compromised systems.
  • Use of ARTEX to exploit a vulnerable custom PHP upload function and stage a web shell, and use it to access secrets and API keys, and ultimately compromise a company's development pipeline to alter a Git repository and deploy an attacker-controlled Kubernetes pod.
